extracted.intended_audience: caption-contest entrants, cartoonists, humor writers, and hobbyist contest followers
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and analytics for producing and evaluating single-panel cartoon captions for caption contests (e.g., The New Yorker, CartoonStock), plus how leaderboards and archives affect submission strategy. Emphasizes matching publication tone, formatting to house style, originality, and using data tools to track performance.

rubrics_metrics.name: TNYCCC Leaderboard ordering ('Larry David–style')
rubrics_metrics.description: In HumorOramaLOL, TNYCCC Leaderboard’s default ordering is ‘Larry David–style': strictly merit-based—no reinterpretations, just total wins, with most recent win as tiebreaker.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ranking metric is total wins; when totals tie, use most recent win as tiebreaker. This is an explicit, merit-focused ordering rule for comparing contestants across contests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match publication tone/personality
rubrics_metrics.description: Caption contests vary widely in tone, and the kinds of captions that win often depend on the personality of the publication hosting the contest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some outlets (e.g., CartoonStock) embrace playful or edgy submissions with innuendo and creative risk; others (e.g., The New Yorker) lean toward a more refined, understated style and avoid anything too risqué or heavy‑handed. Tailor your caption to the host's established voice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow the host's house style formatting
rubrics_metrics.description: The New Yorker follows a specific style guide, and while they may lightly edit winning entries, it’s smart to format your caption the way they prefer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: The New Yorker always prints “O.K.” — never OK, OKAY, or any other variation. Submitting in house style helps your caption feel polished and contest‑ready; expect light edits but make it easy for editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transform the scene with wit, absurdity, or a surprising twist
rubrics_metrics.description: Caption contests invite you to look at a single image and conjure a line that transforms the scene—sometimes with wit, sometimes with absurdity, and often with a surprising twist that makes the whole thing click.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aim for originality that reframes the image; prioritize punch, clarity, and a twist or unexpected angle. Avoid heavy‑handed explanations that kill the subtlety of a single‑line caption.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid clichés and repeat joke-types; research past contests
rubrics_metrics.description: If you're thinking of any 'cross the road' captions this week, have a look at Contests #896, #778, and #55 for those type of captions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before submitting, check archives and past finalists/winners to avoid recycled/overused joke frameworks. Reviewing past contests helps you identify joke types that are stale or already well‑represented.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission polish: make entries contest‑ready
rubrics_metrics.description: Submitting in their house style helps your caption feel polished and contest‑ready from the start.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Beyond house punctuation/abbreviations, ensure concision, readability, and grammatical correctness. Present your caption as you would like it printed—small presentation details can affect perceptions of quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use leaderboards and data tools to analyze performance and trends
rubrics_metrics.description: Leaderboards offer a fun, data‑driven way to see how caption writers and cartoonists stack up across contests, revealing patterns, streaks, surprises, and the occasional underdog surge.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use built‑in tools (pagination, column sorting, search) to dig into rankings and discover insights such as streaks, total wins, and geographical patterns. Treat leaderboard metrics as diagnostics for long‑term improvement rather than single‑entry guarantees.
